title: 1900 was not a leap year, even though it's divisible by 4
assumption: A year is a leap year exactly when it's divisible by 4.

input.display: year % 4 == 0 for 1900 (True) vs the Gregorian rule's actual answer (False)
input.description: A hand-rolled leap-year check (common in date-math utilities, age calculators, or anything that didn't reach for the standard library) applied to any century year.

what_goes_wrong: A hand-written `is_leap(y) = y % 4 == 0` check says 1900 and 2100 are leap years; both are not, and code that trusts the check will construct a nonexistent February 29 or miscount days in centuries not divisible by 400.
why: The Gregorian calendar's actual rule is: divisible by 4 AND (not divisible by 100 OR divisible by 400). Century years are leap only if divisible by 400 -- 1900 and 2100 fail that (divisible by 100, not by 400) and are NOT leap years, while 2000 passes (divisible by 400) and IS one. The simpler 'divisible by 4' rule most developers remember is only an approximation: it is right for 397 of every 400 years and silently wrong for exactly these three century years in each 400.

repros.expected_output:
1900 naive: True actual: False
2000 naive: True actual: True
2024 naive: True actual: True
2100 naive: True actual: False
constructing Feb 29, 1900 raises: day 29 must be in range 1..28 for month 2 in year 1900

1900 naive: true actual: false
2000 naive: true actual: true
2024 naive: true actual: true
2100 naive: true actual: false
new Date(1900, 1, 29) -> 1900 2 1

fix: Use the standard library's leap-year check (Python `calendar.isleap`, or construct the date and catch the error) instead of a hand-rolled `% 4` test. If you must write it yourself, the full rule is `(y % 4 == 0 and y % 100 != 0) or y % 400 == 0`.

sources.title: ISO 8601 / Gregorian calendar leap year rule (Wikipedia, background)

test_cases.note: A correct is_leap_year(1900) must return false.
A correct is_leap_year(2000) must return true.
